Testimony of Thomas Berg

My name is Thomas Berg. I am a minor and lived in my home country with my mother, father, and sibling. In 1998, my parents used all their savings to build a house on land that the government had leased to them. In 2001, the government decided to expropriate the land for a road-widening project and ordered us to remove our house. This was happening to other families in our area as well. My father and several others organized a protest against the expropriation and the lack of fair compensation. As a result, my father and four others were arrested, convicted, and sentenced to three years in jail.

After my father was imprisoned, the government demolished our house. My sibling and I were suspended from school because of our father's political activities and his imprisonment. We were not allowed to return to school while we remained in our home country. The authorities made it clear that our suspension was a direct consequence of our father's actions and his status as a political prisoner. This situation caused us to lose access to education, which is essential for our development and future. We did not know if or when we would be allowed to return to school, as our ability to do so depended on whether our father would be released from prison, which was uncertain.

Because of these events, I fear that if I return to my home country, I will continue to be denied an education and face serious harm due to my relationship to my father, who is considered a political activist by the authorities.

Testimony of Maria Nilsson

My name is Maria Nilsson. I am a citizen of my home country and was living there with my parents, specifically with my father. In March 2002, my father and my uncles decided that I should undergo excision. Their intention was for me to be excised so that I could then be given in marriage to a man who was the same age as my father. This man had chosen me because of his financial resources and his promise to give my father certain property in exchange for my marriage. My mother realized that my father would not be persuaded to abandon this plan. She confided in one of her friends, who held a high position. This friend first arranged for me to move in with her to keep me safe. Later, with her help, I was able to leave my home country. I left in 2002 and arrived in Canada on November 5, 2002. I am afraid to return to my home country because I fear being forced to undergo excision and being forced into marriage against my will. I do not believe I would be able to get protection from the authorities in my home country, as this practice is widespread and deeply rooted in tradition. Even though excision is illegal, no action is taken against those who perform it, and women and girls like me have no real recourse. I was only 12 years old when these events happened, and I do not see any way I could escape my father's actions by living somewhere else in my country. This is why I am seeking protection.

Testimony of Karin Berg

My name is Karin Berg. I am from a region in the north of my home country that was under the control of the national army during the war. In my area, there was forced recruitment of young people by an armed group. In 2006, I was questioned by the army along with other young people and was ordered to report any suspicious activity. I was questioned many times about possible support for the armed group because I am a young Tamil woman. In 2007, I moved to another area, where I completed school and worked, but I returned to my home region in 2009 after the end of the war.

Even after the war ended, Tamils continue to be mistreated in my home country. Militant armed groups abduct and extort people who have relatives abroad, like me. As a young woman, I was very fearful that something bad could happen to me, including the risk of sexual abuse from authorities and militant groups. My home was robbed at gunpoint by Tamil men. I did not fear the particular people who robbed my family home, but I was afraid of members of the military and armed paramilitary groups, who are known to target and sexually assault young Tamil women in the north. I have not personally been subjected to gender-based violence, but my parents told me about other young women facing such mistreatment, and I know that women in my situation are at risk.

Because I am a single young Tamil woman returning from abroad, I face a serious possibility of harassment and sexual assault, including rape, from men involved in military checkpoints throughout my area. There is a high military presence, and as someone who has lived in Canada, I am perceived to have access to money. Even though I am 25 years old, I look young, which makes me more vulnerable. I feared for my safety and decided to leave my home country. I left from the main airport on January 13, 2011, and arrived in Canada on January 14, 2011, where I claimed refugee protection.

Testimony of Anna Larsen

My name is Anna Larsen. I am a 32-year-old citizen of my home country. Together with my husband, I owned and operated a chicken farm in a rural area. On a day in 1995, after we sold all our chickens, we had a large sum of money at home. That evening, a gang of five criminals broke into our house. They killed my husband by forcing mosquito netting down his throat with the butt of a knife, causing him to suffocate. I was present with my husband and our two daughters, who were aged two and five at the time. All of us were gagged and tied up, and my children witnessed the murder. Eventually, my eldest daughter managed to free herself, and the police were called.

The police investigated the incident and, a few months later, asked me to identify the criminals. I was able to positively identify three of the five gang members, who were then detained. The other two were never caught. From 1997 until I left my home country in 2001, I received repeated telephone calls from someone I believed to be one of the two uncaptured criminals. This person threatened to kill me if I gave testimony against the gang. I never testified, but only because the police never asked me to do so.

I reported these threatening calls to the police. They told me they did not have enough manpower to protect me and advised me to avoid going out at night and to keep my doors locked. Despite moving frequently to avoid danger, the threats continued. I feared for my life and the safety of my children. In 2001, I left my home country and came to Canada, seeking protection from the ongoing threats and risk to my life posed by the gang members who killed my husband.

Testimony of Peter Hansen

My name is Peter Hansen. In 2006, I borrowed MXN$40,000 from a man in my home country. I promised to pay the money back later that year. When the time came to repay the loan, I was only able to give him MXN$10,000 because I did not have the full amount. He had me sign an IOU, but it did not state the balance of the principal debt. In 2007, after he cashed the partial payment, he demanded that I pay him MXN$60,000, claiming that the additional amount was interest. When I refused to pay this amount, he became very aggressive toward me. I tried to come to an agreement with him, but he continued to threaten me.

I began to fear for my life because of his threats. My spouse and I moved to several different locations within my home country, but each time, we were tracked down. The threats continued, and I felt that we were not safe anywhere. At one point, I was attacked at gunpoint by this man. He fired shots into the air during the attack, which made me fear that he would kill me. My spouse was also assaulted while I was away.

I went to the Public Prosecutor’s office to file a complaint after receiving death threats, but my complaint was not accepted because I did not have any evidence. After the attack at gunpoint, I did not file another complaint because I believed that the authorities would not assist me unless I had overwhelming evidence. I did not seek help from other federal authorities or human rights organizations because I did not think they would help either.

Fearing for our safety, I left my country on a specific date in 2008 and arrived in Montréal, Canada, the same day. I claimed refugee protection one month later in Montréal. My spouse left our country later in 2008 and arrived in Toronto, where she claimed refugee protection upon arrival at the airport.

Testimony of Peter Hansen

My name is Peter Hansen. I was born and lived my entire life in my home country. In 2014, I was supposed to report for national service, as this would have been the beginning of my final school year. I did not report for national service and instead went into hiding at a friend’s house. I stayed in hiding for about a year. During this time, the authorities came to my parents’ home and searched it, looking for me. My father told the authorities that I had disappeared. I do not know if anything else happened to my family as a result of my absence.

In 2015, a friend of my father, who is a trusted acquaintance, helped me leave my home country. We traveled by car from the capital to a border area, and then we walked across the border into a neighbouring country. From there, we drove to the capital city of that country, where I stayed for almost three months. After that, I flew with a smuggler to Cairo and then onward to Toronto. I used a fraudulent passport to enter Canada. I did not handle the passport myself; the smuggler took care of it and presented it to the officer at the airport. I only saw that the passport was blue, but I do not know the name or nationality on the passport, nor the age or date of birth listed. The smuggler answered all questions from the officer, and I was not asked anything. After entering Canada, the smuggler put me in a taxi and told the driver to take me to a restaurant in a certain neighbourhood. While waiting there, I met an old friend from my home country who recognized me. He gave me shelter for the night and helped me connect with someone who brought me to a lawyer to start my refugee claim.

I fear returning to my home country because I avoided military service and because I have made a refugee claim against the government. If I return, I will face persecution for these reasons.

My name is Peter Hansen. I am a 48-year-old citizen of my home country. I completed ten years of religious schooling. I worked as a merchant in my region, selling rice in bags that had my name printed on them for identification during transportation from the capital, where I purchased the rice, to my town, where I sold it. Because there was a war in my region between the national army and the rebels, and fearing for my life, I returned to live in the capital.

I was flogged four times a day to force me to confess to ties with the rebels. The more I denied any connection, the harsher the treatment became.

With the help of friends, I managed to escape from prison. I then hid for two months. After that, I left my home country using a Canadian visa. If I were to return, I fear that I would be arrested, imprisoned, and tortured by the security forces, who would try to make me confess to complicity with the rebels and force me to give them the names of other people they suspect I know.

Testimony of Thomas Berg

My name is Thomas Berg. In 1998, I wrote a letter addressed to the guerrillas in my home country, urging them to abandon violence and seek peaceful solutions. I tried to have this letter published in a major newspaper, but it was only printed in a small local paper. I also made about 5,000 photocopies, which I distributed to people I knew and posted in public places. In early 2000, after seeing a television program inviting citizens to write to the guerrillas, I sent my letter to the email address provided on the show.

In March 2000, I received a phone call at my apartment from someone who identified themselves as being from an armed group. The caller threatened me, saying that people with big mouths should keep them closed and that I should say goodbye to the world. In 2000, a man in a white car came to our apartment complex and told the porter he was there to pick up my children. Fortunately, my children were not going to school that day, and when my wife went down to meet the man, he left immediately. That same night, I received another threatening call, saying that even if they did not succeed this time, they would succeed next time.

After this, we only left the apartment when necessary and always escorted the children to and from school. Two weeks later, someone else came to the apartment complex asking for the children, but the porter did not provide any information. In June 2000, two men in a white car came to the children’s school and called my daughter by name. She ran inside the school building and only left when her mother arrived and the car was gone. That evening, I received another call, telling me to say goodbye to my daughter. In July 2000, I noticed a motorcycle following me, but I managed to escape.

Because of these threats and attempted kidnappings, I abandoned my business and left my home country with my daughter, traveling to Miami. My wife took our other children to a friend’s house. After two weeks, the callers managed to trace my wife and children at the friend’s place and began calling again, identifying themselves as members of the armed group. My wife and children then joined me in Miami. We later came to Canada and made refugee claims at the border.

Testimony of Peter Hansen

My name is Peter Hansen. I was born in Jaffna, but my family moved to live with relatives when I was an infant due to troubles in my hometown. We returned to Jaffna in 2002 after the road was open following the ceasefire. I completed grade 11 in 2006. From 2007 until 2008, I worked as a labourer in my hometown.

Before finishing school in 2006, the army began rounding up students on Saturdays about once a month. I was picked up during these roundups. In 2007, an army patrol questioned me and told me to sign in regularly at the army camp. One day, an army patrol took my identity card, and I had to go to the army camp to retrieve it. When I got it back, I was told I would have to come back every week to sign in. I usually had to sign in twice a week, sometimes three times. Each time, I was asked the same questions about the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE) and whether I could identify LTTE members. I was also slapped by different people each time. These episodes, occurring regularly for about a year, felt like mental torture to me.

From 2006, there were weekly round-ups where a "head-shaker" would identify LTTE members. On one occasion, ten boys were taken away. Another time, one of my teachers was kidnapped and murdered. After these experiences, I decided I had to leave my home country. I paid 40,000 rupees to a political group for passage to the capital and left Jaffna in 2008. My mother arranged for an agent to get me to Thailand, and I departed my home country in 2008. In Thailand, I registered with the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees. In 2009, the agent took me to another country, where I stayed until I was put on a small boat. On September 3, 2009, I boarded the Ocean Lady and arrived in Canada on October 17, 2009, where I claimed refugee protection at the port of entry.

While in the capital, I was arrested one day before leaving for Thailand because I am a Tamil, and was released only because I could show I had a ticket to Thailand. I fear returning to my home country because I would be suspected of links to the LTTE due to my ethnicity, my history of being questioned and detained, and my journey to Canada on the Ocean Lady, which authorities associate with the LTTE.

Testimony of Thomas Berg

My name is Thomas Berg. My family has a long history as hereditary Chiefs of a tribe in the region where I grew up in my home country. About fifty years ago, my great uncle, concerned that he might not have male descendants, temporarily transferred the Chieftaincy to his brother-in-law. However, the brother-in-law kept the Chieftaincy within his own family, and since then, our two families have been in conflict over who is the legitimate Chief. My father considers himself the rightful Chief and has tried for years to regain the Chieftaincy, but has not succeeded.

Around 1980, a descendant of the brother-in-law assumed the Chieftaincy. I served as secretary to the Town Development Committee during the 1980s and early 1990s. The Chief came under criticism for selling land and not accounting for the proceeds. I acted as the main accuser and, at a public meeting in 1991, demanded that the Chief explain his actions. At that meeting, the Chief threatened to kill me. Initially, I thought it was an empty threat, but three days later, a relative of the Chief warned me that the threat was real. This warning, along with an offer of a teaching position in another town, led me to move away. There, I met and married my wife and raised my children.

During my absence, three people filled in for me at the committee. In 2003, the first died suddenly. In 2004, the second went blind while meeting with the Chief, and later that month, the third became ill with a mysterious disease. These events were caused by the Chief using magic. In 2005, after hearing that my father was seriously ill, I returned with my family to our hometown. I resumed my position with the committee and, together with others, scolded the Chief for trying to get free cement for his personal use. The Chief threatened me again. In 2006, I lodged a complaint against the Chief with the committee and the Council of Elders, who rebuked him. Shortly after, four of the Chief’s nephews confronted and beat me. Friends intervened and chased them away. My maternal uncles reported the incident to the Chief, who blamed me for the beating. One uncle approached the police, but they dismissed the complaint. Members of the committee feared for my safety and urged me to attend a conference in Canada. Once in Canada, I sought protection.

Testimony of Peter Hansen

My name is Peter Hansen. I am a thirty-five year-old citizen of my home country. Between 2000 and 2002, I worked as a photographer for a daily newspaper in my hometown. In the summer of 2000, I took photographs of a man who died under suspicious circumstances in a court building. The newspaper published these photographs. After this, the editor of the paper and I were required to report to the Ministry of Guidance, where we were reprimanded. The authorities then prohibited me from taking photographs in certain areas.

In 2002, I took video and still pictures of New Year celebrations in a part of my hometown. The police arrived to break up the celebrations and detained me along with others. While in custody, the authorities mistreated me and kept me in jail for eight months. When I was released, it was on conditions, and I was required to report to the authorities on several occasions.

After my release, I returned to work with my former editor, who had started a new publication because the authorities had closed the previous newspaper. I became involved in taking photographs at special events at the local university, where I got to know students who opposed the government. Through these contacts, I assisted the students in getting materials printed and helped them distribute those materials at various demonstrations.

In 2003, these students held large public rallies, and I attended some of them. The authorities raided the university and arrested some students who had worked with me. A week later, the police stopped and detained my brother while he was driving my car. They held him for a week and told him they were looking for me because I had participated in demonstrations and helped the student protesters. I became concerned for my safety, believing the authorities may have identified me through photographs taken at the demonstrations or from information given by the arrested students. I went into hiding. With the assistance of one of my brothers and an agent, I left my home country and came to Canada. I fear that if I return, the authorities will detain, torture, and possibly kill me.

Testimony of Thomas Berg

My name is Thomas Berg. I am a 27-year-old man from my home country. I have suffered persecution throughout my life because of my sexual orientation; I am homosexual. Feeling demoralized and desperate to leave my country, I managed to find a job in Oregon, United States, with the help of some friends. I lived in the United States from 2003 to 2004 and tried to legalize my status, but I was unsuccessful. I had to return to my home country to visit my sick mother. After I returned, I witnessed another homosexual being attacked in the street. This incident convinced me that I could not stay any longer. I learned that people like me are protected in Canada, so I decided to leave. I boarded a plane in 2006 and, upon arrival in Montreal, I made a claim for refugee protection.

Testimony of Lars Olsen

My name is Lars Olsen. I am from the north of my home country. My family and I have been repeatedly targeted by the authorities because they suspect us of involvement with an armed group opposed to the government. My father was arrested in 1997, 2001, and 2005. After I finished secondary school, both my twin brother and I were arrested. Other family members were also arrested and tortured during 2005 and 2006. Between 2005 and 2006, I was arrested several times and forced to report weekly to an army camp.

In 2008, I left my hometown and went to the capital to try to find a job abroad. My father gave me the contact of someone who could help me get a visa and a job in Saudi Arabia. When I arrived, I could not reach this person. I stayed in a room arranged by my cousin and shared it with another man who was also planning to go abroad. I lent him my cell phone regularly. During my stay, I was away from the house at times, and the man used my phone.

Early in 2008, the police came to my residence in the capital while I was away. My landlady contacted me and told me that the police had arrested the man who had been using my phone and warned me not to return because the police were also looking for me. I moved to another house and stayed there until I left the country. I flew to Singapore, stayed there for eleven days, and then traveled to Malaysia, where I remained until 2009.

While I was in Malaysia, my mother informed me that my photograph had appeared in a newspaper in my home country, along with ten others, offering a reward for information about me. The article claimed I was involved in importing items for the armed group. After this, my twin brother was arrested, tortured, and questioned about my whereabouts.

On learning this, I applied for refugee status with the United Nations office in Malaysia and was accepted, but I was not given permanent status or allowed to work. I arranged through an agent to travel to Canada by ship. On September 5, 2009, I boarded the ship at sea and arrived in Canada in October 2009.

I fear returning to my home country because I have been publicly identified as a supporter of the armed group, my name and information have appeared in newspapers, and an international notice has been issued for me. If I return, I will be at risk of detention, interrogation, and torture.

Testimony of Peter Hansen

My name is Peter Hansen. I was born and raised in the capital city of my home country, where I lived my entire life until I left. I attended school for 16 years, including a year of university studies, and held several jobs since December 2000. I am single, and in 2002, I began living openly as a homosexual.

My problems started in 2000, when I was beaten by a group of homophobic students at my university. After this attack, I was advised to leave the country, so I went to the United States for five months and worked in Miami. I did not seek protection from authorities there because I believed they would not grant refugee protection based on sexual orientation, and I also experienced violence and discrimination in the United States. I returned to my home country and decided to live openly as a homosexual. My father drove me out of the family home because of his intolerance.

After each attack, my partner and I went to the police, but they refused to listen to us and threatened to detain us for "immoral conduct." My partner and I separated in 2003. Later that year, I began another relationship, which lasted until mid-2003. We were attacked by homophobic individuals while walking hand in hand in a park. When we notified a police officer, he took us to the station and put us in a cell for a few hours for "immoral conduct." On another occasion, neighbours came to our home, attacked us, and told us to leave the neighbourhood. We had to be hospitalized again for a few days.

During this period, I lost my job twice. When I approached the ministry of labour, officials did not want to hear my case. Fearing for my life and unable to find protection, I left my country by plane in 2003, landing in New York the next day. I then travelled by road to the Canadian border, where I immediately expressed my intention to claim refugee protection. I fear that if I return to my home country, I will again be harassed and attacked by neighbours, students, and society at large, including the security forces. I do not believe the authorities in my country are able to provide me with adequate protection.
